draft.title: Radioactive decay
card: An unstable nucleus can change into a more stable one by emitting radiation. This is radioactive decay, and it happens at random.
Alpha
a helium nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons), charge +2. It is heavy and slow, and a sheet of paper or a few centimetres of air stops it.
Beta
a fast electron (beta minus) or positron (beta plus) from the nucleus, with charge -1 or +1. It is very light, and a few millimetres of aluminium stops it.
Gamma
a high-energy photon from the nucleus. It has no charge and no mass, and it is the most penetrating. Thick lead or concrete is needed to reduce it.
draft.remember: Alpha is heavy and stopped easily, beta is light and moderate, gamma is uncharged and the most penetrating.

a.q: Which type of radiation has no charge and is the most penetrating?
a.why: Gamma rays are photons, so they carry no charge, and they pass through paper and aluminium. Beta particles are charged and are stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium, so they penetrate less.
a.clue: Think of the one that is a photon, not a particle with mass.

b.q: A radioactive source is placed behind a sheet of paper. A detector behind the paper still records radiation, but it drops to near zero when a few millimetres of aluminium is added. What is the source emitting?
b.why: Radiation passes the paper, so it is not alpha, which paper stops. Aluminium of a few millimetres stops it, so it is not gamma, which would still get through. This fits beta particles.
b.clue: Which radiation passes paper but not thin aluminium?

problems.detail: The why says the source is 'not alpha, which paper stops'. That reasoning is wrong: paper would stop any alpha before the detector, so the experiment cannot show whether the source also emits alpha. It only shows that what reaches the detector is beta. This teaches a faulty inference.
'Beta particles only' overclaims, because the setup cannot rule out alpha. The question should ask what radiation reaches the detector, or the option should read 'Beta particles' without 'only'.
The clue ('the one that is a photon') gives the answer away, because the card names gamma as the photon.

check.summary: Question b's explanation wrongly says the source cannot emit alpha, since paper would stop any alpha anyway, so 'Beta particles only' overclaims. Reword it to ask what reaches the detector. Question a's clue also nearly gives the answer away.

b.q: A radioactive source is placed behind a sheet of paper. A detector behind the paper records radiation, but the count drops to near zero when a few millimetres of aluminium is added. What radiation is reaching the detector?
